items.stem: Which communication style does the .NET microservices guidance recommend for propagating changes across multiple services?

options.text: Asynchronous messaging via an event bus
options.rationale: Correct: publish/subscribe messaging decouples services when propagating updates.
Chatty synchronous calls perform poorly and couple services.

options.text: A shared database all services write to
options.rationale: A shared database breaks service autonomy.
Services run in separate processes; in-process calls are not possible.

items.explanation: Correct: publish/subscribe messaging decouples services when propagating updates.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about data in a microservices architecture are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Each microservice typically owns its own data store
Cross-service consistency is usually eventual, not atomic
options.rationale: Correct: atomic transactions across services are generally not possible.

options.text: All services should share one relational database for consistency
options.rationale: A shared database couples services and breaks autonomy.

options.text: Two-phase commit across services is the recommended default
options.rationale: Distributed transactions are avoided; eventual consistency is preferred.

items.explanation: Correct: services own their data and consistency across them is eventual.

items.stem: A small team with a simple, stable application is considering microservices. What does the guidance suggest?

options.text: Microservices add operational complexity and suit large, complex, evolving systems rather than simple ones
options.rationale: Correct: the added complexity is only worth it for large, complex applications.

options.text: Always choose microservices because they are more modern
options.rationale: Architecture choice depends on the system, not fashion.
They increase deployment and operational complexity.

options.text: Microservices require no changes to communication
options.rationale: Moving to services changes in-process calls to network calls.

items.explanation: Correct: the added complexity is only worth it for large, complex applications.
